The offensive was coordinated with Iran’s Revolutionary Guards, which also provided additional weapons support.
entries.why_it_matters: Trump’s war with Iran is creating economic chaos with no end in sight. Two of the world’s most important shipping routes are now under threat, pushing energy and shipping costs even higher.

entries.what_happened: An Iranian missile attack on a U.S. air base in Jordan damaged an A-10 and eight F-15 fighter jets, according to a U.S. official. American forces fired about 30 Patriot interceptors during the attack as the military faces growing concerns over depleted air-defense stockpiles after six months of war with Iran.

The U.S. skipped a NATO meeting of an international group it helped create to reduce civilian casualties in war. This comes after Pete Hegseth dismantled much of the Pentagon program focused on civilian harm. Staffing has dropped from nearly 200 people to about two dozen, despite objections from senior military commanders.
entries.why_it_matters: The U.S. is walking away from safeguards meant to protect civilians during military operations. With American forces involved in conflicts across the Middle East, dismantling those protections puts civilians at even greater risk.

entries.what_happened: U.S. and Middle Eastern officials say Iran is producing ballistic missiles again despite U.S. and Israeli strikes that badly damaged its missile industry. Iran is using stockpiled components and assembling missiles at underground facilities. Production is still below previous levels, but Iran is building new underground sites and is believed to have thousands of ballistic missiles left.

The U.S. is pushing NATO allies to leave the treaty that created the International Criminal Court and help “systematically dismantle” it, according to three NATO diplomats. U.S. Ambassador to NATO Matthew Whitaker reportedly warned them, “We will be watching closely who stands with America.” DOJ has also confirmed that the U.S. rejects the court’s jurisdiction over Americans.
entries.why_it_matters: The ICC prosecutes genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity when countries fail to do it. Dismantling the court would make it much harder to hold people accountable for some of the world’s most horrific crimes.

entries.what_happened: Britain, Norway and the U.S. tracked and confronted Russian vessels near Svalbard after detecting an operation by Russia’s secretive GUGI undersea warfare unit. Russian deep-sea submersibles were testing new technology designed to disable critical subsea cables without leaving evidence behind. NATO allies stopped the vessels from completing the exercise, and no cables were damaged.

U.S. wholesale inflation accelerated to 5.4% in August, up from 4.8% in July, as rising energy costs pushed prices higher. Energy prices jumped 4.2% in a single month, including a 24.1% surge in diesel prices.
entries.why_it_matters: Businesses are paying more for energy and transportation, and those costs will be passed down to consumers. Americans already dealing with higher gas and energy prices will soon see those increases show up in the cost of everyday goods.

entries.what_happened: The national average price of diesel surpassed $6 a gallon for the first time due to Trump’s war with Iran. Brent crude climbed above $107 a barrel, while U.S. diesel inventories remain 13% below their five-year average.
Around 150 protesters marched outside the Republican National Committee’s midterm convention in Dallas to protest against Trump’s Iran war and immigration crackdown.

entries.what_happened: Trump rejected the idea of regulating the artificial intelligence industry, calling warnings about safety a “HOAX.” Trump claimed that “the only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT,” adding: “We already have tremendous CRIMINAL and REGULATORY power over these companies!” His comments came after Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei urged AI companies to “slow the pace” of development and called for government rules requiring independent audits of frontier models. That position was also endorsed by OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and xAI CEO Elon Musk. Trump, however, singled out Amodei, claiming he had already stopped AI “people” from doing “bad, or potentially bad, ‘things,’ like Dario (Anthropic!), who is now pretending to be a ‘perfect little angel,’” and claimed that efforts to limit the technology were part of a “SICK conspiracy” in which “the only one that is happy about it is China. WHOEVER WINS AI, WINS!”

House Speaker Mike Johnson said Congress “potentially” will need to impose guardrails on AI, but warned that legislation could take “some time.” Congress, however, is unlikely to pass broad AI safety legislation before the midterm elections, with the House scheduled to leave Washington this week and not return until November. Johnson argued that companies should bear responsibility for providing safe products and warned that “hyper-regulation” could undermine the U.S. advantage over China.

The EPA repealed Biden-era greenhouse gas limits on coal- and gas-fired power plants and proposed a separate rule to prevent future administrations from restoring them. The EPA claimed that power-plant greenhouse gases don’t “significantly contribute” to dangerous pollution and therefore don’t meet the Clean Air Act threshold for regulation. Power plants, however, are the nation’s second-largest source of carbon dioxide emissions. The EPA estimates that revoking the standards would save the energy industry more than $300 billion. The Biden administration had estimated that its rule would produce $370 billion in climate and public-health benefits.

Trump called for the U.S. to have “the lowest interest rate in the world.” Fed Chair Kevin Warsh, however, is expected to raise rates this week after inflation rose 0.4% in August and oil climbed above $100 a barrel. The 10-year Treasury yield also briefly hit 5%, its highest level since October 2023, pushing mortgage and other borrowing costs higher as heavy AI investments and borrowing have added to demand for capital.

House Speaker Mike Johnson confirmed that Trump’s promised $5,000 payments to Americans require congressional approval. Congress, however, hasn’t committed to the payments, and Johnson added “we have had zero time, of course, to process that, deliberate, discuss it.” Trump, nevertheless, insisted that the checks were “going forward” and that the government could “easily handle” the cost. Sending $5,000 to every U.S. adult could cost about $1.3 trillion.

A second federal judge blocked Trump’s attempt to restrict mail-in voting for the midterm election. U.S. District Judge Carl Nichols, a Trump appointee, found that “no statute grants the Postal Service the power” to refuse to deliver mail-in ballots in states that don’t upload voter lists or use envelope barcodes. Nichols warned that allowing the rule could leave “a significant number of absentee or mail-in ballots will ultimately not be counted.” The Supreme Court, meanwhile, is considering the Trump administration’s request to lift a separate injunction issued by a federal judge in Boston.

New York and 21 other states sued the Trump administration to block its new “public charge” rule, which would give immigration officials wider discretion to deny green cards and visas based on applicants’ use of public benefits. The states argued that the Department of Homeland Security exceeded its authority because Congress never changed the longstanding definition of who is considered a “public charge.” The rule is set to take effect Friday. DHS estimates that more than 950,000 people could disenroll from or decline to enroll in public benefits as a result.

The Department of Homeland Security’s inspector general found that Florida’s now-closed “Alligator Alcatraz” detention center confined immigrants in small metal cages. At least 79 detainees spent nearly two hours in small enclosures that staff described as “calming areas.” Investigators called the use of cages “highly unconventional” and posed “significant risks” to detainees’ health and safety. At least one enclosure may have been used as punishment. The watchdog also found detainees lived in cramped, windowless units, lacked daily access to showers, and encountered bug-infested facilities.
Mitch McConnell returned to the U.S. Capitol and voted for the first time in three months. McConnell, 84, was hospitalized in June after a fall.

A Russian oligarch spent hundreds of thousands to sponsor two nights of celebrations for Trump Jr.’s Bahamas wedding. Trump Jr. and his wife, Bettina Anderson, confirmed that “our dear friend” Umar Kremlev “very generously hosted two incredible nights of celebrations for us” after their May 22 family-only ceremony, calling it an “extraordinarily generous wedding gift from a friend.” Kremlev was awarded Russia’s Order of Friendship by Putin in April and has been sanctioned by Ukraine over his ties to the Kremlin. Meanwhile, Trump, who didn’t attend his son’s wedding, said, “I have no idea who Umar is, never heard of him.”

The Supreme Court blocked Trump’s plan to limit mail-in voting in the midterms, saying the administration was “unlikely to succeed on the merits” of its challenge. Justice Brett Kavanaugh wrote that while there was “at least a fair prospect” the Postal Service had statutory authority to issue the rules, applying them this year “would be arbitrary and capricious” because election officials didn’t have “sufficient time to reasonably implement” them. The changes would have required states to submit lists of voters eligible to receive mail ballots and redesign ballot envelopes with unique barcodes, allowing the Postal Service to return noncompliant ballot mail to election officials even though its required online portal wasn’t operational yet.

Trump attacked the Supreme Court over its “bad decision” to block his restrictions on mail-in voting, calling the ruling “a big loss for Republicans, and America itself.” He claimed without evidence that it would make cheating on mail ballots easier. “The Supreme Court has really let our Country down!” Trump said, adding that “These are not the people I interviewed to serve on the United States Supreme Court.” After singling out his three appointees – Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh, and Amy Coney Barrett – Trump praised Justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas for dissenting, calling them “legends both.”

FBI Director Kash Patel declined to rule out sending agents to polling places during the November midterm elections. “I don’t know that we can’t legally do it,” Patel told the Senate Judiciary Committee. Added, however, that the FBI would “follow the law” and that “if there’s a reason to go there, because there’s been a violation of law, we will, otherwise we won’t.” Patel said the bureau would “house our agents and intel analysts in our field offices” and keep election-crime coordinators at all 56 field offices because “election integrity is of paramount importance” and “this FBI is not going to shy away from that effort.” Federal law, however, bars armed federal officers or military personnel from polling places except in limited circumstances. When Sen. Peter Welch asked Patel to pledge that he wouldn’t interfere with voters, Patel replied: “I pledge unequivocally that I will not participate in your charade of lies.”

The Congressional Budget Office estimates that Trump’s war with Iran has cost the U.S. about $38 billion, and that it will continue to cost roughly $2 billion to $3 billion a month for as long as the fighting continues. The nonpartisan budget office also expects the war to add about .05 percentage points to inflation in the first quarter of 2027 due to disruptions to oil and natural gas shipments through the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea. The CBO report blamed the war for more than 40% of inflation during the second quarter of 2026. The Pentagon, however, didn’t provide information requested by the CBO, which acknowledged that the missing data limited its analysis and excluded the cost of repairing damaged U.S. bases.

The Senate blocked a cryptocurrency regulation bill that would have established a federal regulatory framework for digital assets. The Clarity Act, which would have divided oversight of digital assets between the SEC and CFTC, failed to clear the 60-vote threshold after every Democrat and several Republicans opposed advancing it. Democrats argued that the revised ethics provisions still didn’t do enough to prevent Trump and other federal officials from profiting from crypto holdings while overseeing policies that could affect their value. Last year, Trump reported more than $1.4 billion in income from crypto ventures. And in 2024, the crypto industry spent more than $130 million in congressional races to elect pro-crypto legislators.

The Kennedy Center’s board voted to immediately close the performing arts venue for renovations after a federal judge again blocked an effort to put Trump’s name on the building. U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper ruled that the board “cannot install memorials for President Trump or anyone or anything else at the Kennedy Center without Congress’s blessing.” Trump, meanwhile, threatened that “the Reconstruction and the Renovation of The Kennedy Center will not take place” unless his name is on it. He also claimed the center was in a “virtual state of collapse,” called Cooper “very hostile and conflicted,” and said he raised $17 million that’s been deposited into the center’s account “to keep it afloat.”

The U.S. confirmed that it has “on-orbit space control weapons” capable of defending American forces. The Space Force said the weapons can be used for “offensive and defensive purposes.” China, meanwhile, accused the U.S. of “preparing for war in outer space” and warned against an arms race, while Russia called for space to remain “free of any weapon.”

The Federal Reserve raised interest rates for the first time since 2023 and signaled that another hike could come this year as inflation remains above the Fed’s 2% target. The unanimous quarter-point increase lifted the benchmark rate to a range of 3.75% to 4%. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh warned that “the plain fact is that inflation is too high and has been for too long,” adding that inflation hadn’t improved enough to justify holding rates steady. Trump, meanwhile, demanded that rates be cut to “1%, or less” and that the Fed “LOWER THE INTEREST RATES FOR THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA, AND FAST!”

The Trump administration paid federal employees $9.5 billion not to work during 2025 as part of the DOGE effort to cut costs by shrinking the government. The Government Accountability Office estimated that $6.7 billion came from the deferred resignation program, which allowed nearly 140,000 federal workers to stop working while continuing to receive pay and benefits through September before resigning or retiring. The Office of Personnel Management called the $9.5 billion a “one-time expense” and claimed that the workforce reductions will save taxpayers $40 billion a year. The so-called Department of Government Efficiency’s goal was to cut government spending by $1 trillion.

The House voted for a third time to direct Trump to end the war in Iran. Seven Republicans joined Democrats in support of the resolution, which directs the Trump administration to “remove United States Armed Forces from hostilities against the Islamic Republic of Iran” except for personnel needed to defend U.S. or allied bases in the Middle East. However, it’s unclear whether the Senate will take up the measure before the midterms.

Republican Rep. Thomas Massie introduced eight articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Massie accused Hegseth of defying Congress and illegally continuing the U.S. war in Iran without congressional authorization, allowing an “unlawful war” to continue. He also accused Hegseth of ignoring laws to minimize civilian casualties, ordering extrajudicial killings, retaliating against Democratic Sen. Mark Kelly for criticizing military orders, “kidnapping a sovereign leader” in Venezuela, and waging an unlawful war in Yemen. “In all of this, Secretary Hegseth has acted in a manner contrary to his trust as Secretary of Defense,” Massie said on the House floor. The Pentagon, meanwhile, defended Hegseth as a “transformative leader” and maintained that the “entire Department is unified behind the Secretary’s vision.”

House Speaker Mike Johnson canceled votes and sent lawmakers home, delaying the vote on impeaching Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth until after the November elections. By sending lawmakers home a day early for its planned seven-week preelection recess, it pushed action on Rep. Thomas Massie’s impeachment resolution until lawmakers return Nov. 9. Massie’s resolution to impeach Hegseth was “privileged,” meaning the House would was required to act on it no later than Thursday. Johnson denied that the schedule change was to avoid the Hegseth vote, called the impeachment effort a “publicity stunt,” and said it would be tabled when the House returns.
